label: r03-E-T1-4
response:
# SPE Round r01 plan: triage agent

This is round r01. There is no `spe/` folder and no agent yet, so this round builds both and runs the first eval. I assumed the 40 tickets live in `data/eval/tickets.jsonl` with the support lead's labels in the same file. Step 2 splits them into a text file and a separate label file.

## 1. Specify

Your spec is "triage tickets correctly and cheaply." The words "correctly" and "cheaply" need numbers. I picked the defaults below and logged each one in `spe/spec/disagreements.md`. You can change any of them before you approve.

### Requirement table (r01)

| ID | Requirement | Source | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | The agent reads one ticket and returns JSON with `category`, `priority`, and `reply`. | User: "triage tickets" | Code check. The output parses against `triage/schema.json`. |
| R2 | `category` is one of billing, bug, how-to, account, outage. | Project brief | Code check. The value is in the enum. |
| R3 | `priority` is one of P1, P2, P3, P4. | Project brief | Code check. The value is in the enum. |
| R4 | Category matches the support lead's label on at least 85% of tickets. | Default for "correctly" | Code check. Exact match against `labels.jsonl`. |
| R5 | Priority is within one level of the label on at least 90% of tickets. | Default for "correctly" | Code check. The absolute difference is 1 or less. |
| R6 | Every ticket labeled P1 gets P1. A missed P1 is the costliest error. | Default for "correctly" | Code check. P1 recall equals 1.0. |
| R7 | The draft reply answers the customer's actual question. It promises no refund, credit, date, or SLA, and it asks for missing details when needed. | Default for "drafts a first reply" | Code check first: a regex flags promise words, and the length must be 40 to 250 words. Then a rubric judge scores the rest as pass or fail. |
| R8 | "Cheaply" means the lowest mean cost per ticket among configs that meet R4, R5, and R6. | Default for "cheaply" | Code check. The harness sums token usage times list price per ticket. |
| R9 | The agent sees only the ticket text. It never sees labels, graders, or predictions. | SPE rule | Code check. A transcript scan voids any trial that read those paths. |

There are no proposals from a previous round to adopt or reject.

### Open decisions (owner: you, or the support lead through you)

| ID | Decision | Default I logged |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | The correctness bar in R4 to R6 | 0.85 category, 0.90 within-one priority, 1.0 P1 recall |
| D2 | The cost ceiling per ticket | No hard ceiling. The cheapest passing config wins. |
| D3 | Whether the support lead must review the reply rubric | I write it now. The support lead reviews it before round r02. |
| D4 | The model IDs | `claude-sonnet-4-5` is the pinned reference and `claude-haiku-4-5` is the cheaper arm. I will confirm the current IDs and prices in the docs before the dry run. |

## 2. Predict

### Configurations

Each config changes one thing from C0.

| Config | Model | Prompt | What changed from C0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| C0 (reference) | claude-sonnet-4-5 | Zero-shot. Category and priority definitions only. | Nothing |
| C1 | claude-haiku-4-5 | Same as C0 | Model only |
| C2 | claude-sonnet-4-5 | C0 plus 5 few-shot examples. I write the examples from the definitions. None of them come from the 40 eval tickets. | Prompt only |

Each config runs 3 trials per ticket, which is 120 trials per config. A hit means the measured value falls inside the band. Each band is about 1.5 standard errors for n=40.

### Prediction table

| Metric | C0 | C1 | C2 | Grader check | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Schema-valid rate | 1.00 ± 0.02 | 0.98 ± 0.03 | 1.00 ± 0.02 | `check_schema` | Structured output is reliable on both models. Haiku sometimes drifts on enums. |
| Category accuracy | 0.85 ± 0.08 | 0.80 ± 0.08 | 0.88 ± 0.08 | `check_category_exact` | Bug and outage overlap, and so do account and billing. That costs about 6 tickets. Examples help a little. |
| Priority exact match | 0.60 ± 0.10 | 0.55 ± 0.10 | 0.65 ± 0.10 | `check_priority_exact` | The support lead's P2 versus P3 choices follow unwritten rules that the prompt cannot fully capture. |
| Priority within one level | 0.90 ± 0.07 | 0.87 ± 0.07 | 0.92 ± 0.07 | `check_priority_within1` | Most priority misses are off by one level. |
| P1 recall | 0.80 ± 0.20 | 0.70 ± 0.20 | 0.85 ± 0.20 | `check_p1_recall` | I expect about 5 P1 tickets, so one miss moves the number by 0.20. Outages that customers phrase calmly will get P2. |
| Reply pass rate | 0.85 ± 0.10 | 0.75 ± 0.10 | 0.88 ± 0.10 | `check_reply_rules` first, then `judge_reply` | Billing replies will sometimes promise a refund. Haiku does this more often. |
| Mean cost per ticket (USD) | 0.013 ± 0.004 | 0.0045 ± 0.0015 | 0.016 ± 0.005 | `cost_from_usage` | About 2,300 input tokens and 400 output tokens at list price. The examples add about 1,000 input tokens. |

The naive baseline is "always the most common category, always the most common priority." Code computes it from the labels, so it has no prediction. The prediction log will say plainly if it beats any config.

`same_as_last_round` is null for every number because this is round r01.

### Which config I expect to win

I expect no config to meet R6 (P1 recall 1.0). That would make D1 the main question for round r02. Among the configs, I expect C2 to have the best accuracy and C1 to have the lowest cost.

## 3. Evaluate

### Steps after you approve (local commit after each step, no push)

1. **Save the plan and the prediction.** Create `spe/spec/transcripts/2026-10-21-r01.md` with your prompt word for word. Create `spe/spec/spec.md` with the table above, `spe/spec/disagreements.md` with D1 to D4, and `spe/plans/r01.md` with this plan. Write `spe/predictions/r01.yaml`. Its first line is `# Saved before the eval ran. Do not edit after the run.` It lists round, date, author ("Claude, approved by the user in plan mode"), configs, every number with its band and Why, and `same_as_last_round: null`. Commit message: `spe r01: spec, plan, and prediction`.
2. **Split the data.** Write `spe/evals/data/tickets.jsonl` with ID and text only. Write `spe/evals/data/labels.jsonl` with ID, category, and priority. Commit message: `spe r01: split eval tickets from labels`.
3. **Build the agent.** Write `triage/prompt.md`, `triage/examples.md`, `triage/schema.json`, and `triage/run.js`. The runner takes one ticket and a config name. Commit message: `triage: first agent with schema output`.
4. **Build the graders.** Write `spe/evals/graders/` with the code checks named in the table and the reply judge rubric. The judge model is claude-sonnet-4-5 at temperature 0. It sees the ticket and the reply, but not the config name. Commit message: `spe r01: graders and reply rubric`.
5. **Gate 1: grader selftest.** The oracle (labels copied as answers, plus a hand-written good reply) must pass every check. An empty output and a wrong output (every ticket "how-to, P4", with a reply that promises a refund) must fail. If any check gets this wrong, I halt and report.
6. **Gate 2: control regrade.** There is no earlier round to regrade. I logged this as a default. The selftest oracle and the naive baseline are the control for r01.
7. **Gate 3: dry run.** I run C0 and C1 on 3 tickets each, 1 trial each, which is 6 trials. The dry run passes when the schema parses, every grader returns a result, cost is logged, and the transcript scan finds no reads of `labels.jsonl`, `graders/`, or `spe/predictions/`.
8. **Launch the Workflow.** Script: `spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js`.

### Workflow arguments

| Argument | Value |
|---|---|
| `ROUND` | `"r01"`, held in one constant and used everywhere else |
| `configs` | `["C0", "C1", "C2"]` |
| `tickets` | `spe/evals/data/tickets.jsonl` (40 tickets) |
| `trials_per_cell` | 3 |
| `split_cell_extra_trials` | Up to 2 more trials when the 3 trials on a ticket disagree on category or priority. The cap is 60 extra trials per config. |
| `budget_cap_usd` | 25.00. The harness skips and logs any trial that would cross the cap. |
| `trial_access` | Ticket text only. No repository read access. |
| `final_steps` | Failure analysis that groups misses into F-numbered types, then a completeness critic that checks every predicted cell has a measured value |

### Cost estimate (unmeasured)

The base runs are 360 trials. They cost about $1.60 for C0, $0.55 for C1, and $1.90 for C2, so about $4.05. The reply judge adds about $0.01 per trial, which is about $3.60. Split cells could add up to $3. The estimated total is about $8 to $11. The $25 cap leaves room for one rerun.

### Halt conditions

I will halt and report if the budget cap is hit, if any trial reads an answer key, if a grader turns out to be broken, or if a decision only you can make comes up. I will never push, deploy, or send anything.

### Close-out after the completion notice

- `spe/prediction-log.md` gets every metric and config with predicted, measured, verdict, and closer. A "Which Why broke" section follows it.
- `spe/failures.md` gets each new failure type with its F number.
- `spe/spec/spec.md` gets a "Proposed for round r02" table. `spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml` gets `status: draft`.
- `spe/README.md` gets updated. I commit locally and tag the round. Commit message: `spe r01: learn`.

The prediction table gives numbers with bands for each of C0, C1, and C2. Examples are "0.85 ± 0.08" and "0.0045 ± 0.0015". The table uses no adjectives in place of numbers.
Every metric row has a Why column that explains the numbers and the differences between configs. Examples are "Bug and outage overlap... Examples help a little" and "Haiku does this more often."
